docs.title: Your chosen setup in plain words
docs.content:
## Your chosen setup: One Hetzner Cloud server (CPX02: 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM), excl. VAT

**In plain words.** You rent one small computer in a data centre and your app runs on it. It's like renting a flat yourself instead of staying in a hotel with staff.

**Cost.** About 6.49 EUR per month, from the report's price table (prices read 2026-10-24). Taxes, traffic charges and anything the report doesn't list aren't included.

**If the machine or its data centre has a problem:** this stops until it's fixed or recreated, because everything runs in one place.

**What you get**

- The lowest price in this list.
- Easy to understand: one machine runs your app, with no cluster or extra services to learn.
- A simple bill: it is mostly the price of the one machine you rent.
- Quick to set up: the download has what it takes to create the server and start your app.
- No lock-in: your app runs in plain Docker, so you can move it to another provider later.

**Why it costs what it does.** You only pay for the machine. The pricier options also pay for spare copies of your app, for switching over when something fails, and for someone else keeping it all running. Here none of that comes with it, so it costs less and that work lands on you.

**What you give up**

- If the machine breaks or restarts, your app is down until you sort it out. Nothing switches over by itself.
- Updates and security patches are yours to install.
- Backups are off unless you turn them on, and Hetzner charges extra for them.
- It can't grow by itself: a sudden rush makes it slow, and a bigger project will outgrow one machine.

**A good fit if:**

- A first launch, a side project or an internal tool
- Small, steady traffic
- A team that can log into a server and fix things

**Think again if:**

- You've promised customers almost no downtime
- Losing recent data would really hurt
- Nobody on the team is comfortable with a server
- Traffic is big or hard to predict

**Before you launch**

- Turn on backups, then restore one to see that it works.
- Set up an uptime alert, so you hear about it when the site is down.
- Pick a regular time to install updates.
- Keep the Terraform files: they can create the same machine again if you lose it (your data is separate).

**How this choice changes the gaps in your report**

- `no_observability`: Matters more on one machine, because nobody restarts it for you. Add an uptime alert before you launch.

**What the download adds for this choice**

- `infra/hetzner/main.tf`
- `infra/hetzner/variables.tf`
- `infra/hetzner/outputs.tf`
- `infra/hetzner/cloud-init.yaml`
- `infra/hetzner/terraform.tfvars.example`
- `infra/hetzner/.gitignore`
- `docker-compose.prod.yml`
- `deploy/Caddyfile`

**Links**

- [Hetzner Cloud: servers and prices](https://www.hetzner.com/cloud/)

docs.title: What to do with these files, step by step
docs.content:
# How to put this into practice

For your choice: **One Hetzner Cloud server (CPX02: 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM), excl. VAT**.

These steps were written from a fixed template, with the names from the scan of your project filled in. **Nothing here was run against your project or your cloud account.** Do the steps in order and check that each one worked before you start the next.

## Before you start

- Your project is in a git repository that you can push to (GitHub, for example).
- Docker is installed on your computer, so you can test the image before it goes anywhere.
- A Hetzner Cloud account (https://www.hetzner.com/cloud/) and a project in it.
- Terraform 1.5 or newer (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install).

## Step 1: Copy the files into your project

Work on a new branch so nothing can break your main one:

```
git switch -c add-infraloop-files
```

Copy the files from this download into your project. They are laid out like your project, so keep the folders as they are.

- `.dockerignore`: .dockerignore for the repository root
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: GitHub Actions workflow (build and test)
- `.github/dependabot.yml`: Dependabot configuration
- `.env.example`: .env.example (names only)
- `infra/hetzner/main.tf`: Terraform: server, SSH key and firewall
- `infra/hetzner/variables.tf`: Terraform: variables
- `infra/hetzner/outputs.tf`: Terraform: outputs
- `infra/hetzner/cloud-init.yaml`: Server start-up script (cloud-init)
- `infra/hetzner/terraform.tfvars.example`: Terraform: example values
- `infra/hetzner/.gitignore`: Keeps Terraform state and your values out of git
- `docker-compose.prod.yml`: docker-compose file for the server
- `deploy/Caddyfile`: Reverse proxy configuration

On a Mac, Finder hides names that start with a dot (`.github`, `.dockerignore`, `.env.example`). Press `Cmd + Shift + .` in Finder to show them, or copy with your code editor or the terminal.

If a file with the same name already exists in your project, **do not overwrite it**. Open both, compare them, and keep what you need. InfraLoop never edits files you already have. `MANIFEST.md` also lists 2 fixes for files you already have, to make by hand.

## Step 2: Check that the image builds on your computer

For each service, build the image and start it. A service that fails here would fail on a server too, so fix it now:

**app** (`Dockerfile`):

```
docker build -t app .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env app
```

The app reads these variables: `ELASTICSEARCH_URL`, `LOG_TO_STDOUT`, `MAIL_PASSWORD`, `MAIL_PORT`, `MAIL_SERVER`, `MAIL_USERNAME`, `MAIL_USE_TLS`, `MS_TRANSLATOR_KEY`, `REDIS_URL`, `SECRET_KEY`, `SERVER_NAME`. `.env.example` lists the names. Copy it to `.env`, fill in test values, and keep `.env` out of git (it is in the generated `.dockerignore`; add it to `.gitignore` too).

Then open `http://localhost:8000` in a browser (the port is the one the template assumed: change it if your app listens on another). If it does not answer, read the output of `docker run`: it usually says what is missing.

## Step 3: Turn on the checks

Commit the files and push the branch:

```
git add -A
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, CI and deployment files"
git push -u origin add-infraloop-files
```

Open your repository on GitHub and look at the **Actions** tab. The workflow builds and tests your code and builds the image. It does not deploy anything. If it fails, the log says which step; the most common causes are a wrong branch name in the file or a missing test command.

Open a pull request, let the checks pass, then merge it.

## Step 4: Create the server on Hetzner Cloud

### 4a. Get ready

In the Hetzner Cloud console open your project, then Security, then API tokens, and create a token with **Read & Write** access. Copy it once: it is not shown again.
In the terminal where you will run Terraform, set it as a variable (it stays in that terminal and is never written to a file):
```
export TF_VAR_hcloud_token='paste-the-token-here'
```

### 4b. Make an SSH key (skip this if you already have one)

```
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

The last command prints one line (the public key). You will paste it into the next step. Never share the other file, `id_ed25519`.

### 4c. Make sure the server can download your project

The new server fetches your project from git, so the files from steps 1 to 3 must already be on the branch it downloads (`main` unless you change `branch`), and the repository must be public or readable without a password. For a private repository this pack does not work as it is: see the notes in `MANIFEST.md`.

### 4d. Fill in your values

```
cd infra/hetzner
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars
```

Open `terraform.tfvars` and set `ssh_public_key` (the line you printed), `admin_cidrs` (your own public address followed by `/32`, for example `["203.0.113.4/32"]`; find it with `curl -s https://ifconfig.me`) and `repo_url` (the HTTPS address of your repository). That file is git-ignored on purpose. SSH stays closed to everyone else.

### 4e. Create it

```
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan
```

Read the plan. It should create about 3 things (an SSH key, a firewall and the server) and change nothing else. If it wants to change or destroy something you did not expect, stop and ask before going on. Then:

```
terraform apply
```

Type `yes` when it asks. When it finishes it prints `server_ip` and `url`.

### 4f. Wait, then look

The first start takes a few minutes: the server installs Docker, downloads your project and builds the image. Then open the address:

```
terraform output url
```

You will see your app, or an error page from the reverse proxy if the app is still starting or is missing its settings (next step).

### 4g. Give the app its settings

The settings are created as empty names so that no secret passes through Terraform or Hetzner Cloud's start-up data. Log in and fill them in:

```
ssh root@<server_ip>
sudo nano /opt/app/.env
cd /opt/app && sudo docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d
```

Names to fill in: `ELASTICSEARCH_URL`, `LOG_TO_STDOUT`, `MAIL_PASSWORD`, `MAIL_PORT`, `MAIL_SERVER`, `MAIL_USERNAME`, `MAIL_USE_TLS`, `MS_TRANSLATOR_KEY`, `REDIS_URL`, `SECRET_KEY`, `SERVER_NAME`.

### 4h. If something is wrong

```
ssh root@<server_ip>
sudo cloud-init status
sudo tail -n 60 /var/log/cloud-init-output.log
sudo docker compose -f /opt/app/docker-compose.prod.yml logs --tail 60
```

The first command says whether the first start finished. The second shows what the start-up script did. The third shows what your app printed.

### 4i. Your own domain and HTTPS (optional)

1. In your domain's DNS settings, create an **A record** that points at `server_ip`.
2. Wait until it resolves (`nslookup app.example.com`).
3. On the server, set `SITE_ADDRESS=app.example.com` in `/opt/app/.env`, then run `cd /opt/app && sudo docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d`. The proxy gets a free certificate by itself.

Do not change `domain` in `terraform.tfvars` after the first `apply` just for this: it changes the start-up script, and Terraform will then want to restart or replace the server. Read `terraform plan` before you agree to anything like that.

## Step 5: Before you call it done

- Open the address from a different network (your phone, off Wi-Fi) to check it is reachable from outside.
- Set an uptime alert, so you hear when the site is down.
- Turn on backups and **restore one** to see that it works.
- Set a budget alert with your provider, so a surprise cost reaches you.
- Keep `MANIFEST.md` somewhere your team can find it: it lists what each file assumed and what to check.

## Taking it down again

Everything Terraform created can be removed with one command. It destroys the server and its data, so copy anything you need first:

```
cd infra/hetzner
terraform destroy
```

## If you get stuck

Check `MANIFEST.md`: every file has a "Check before you use it" list, and the most common problems are on it. Prices and server names change over time, so check the provider's own page before you rely on a number.

docs.title: What each file assumes and what to check
docs.content:
# Files generated by InfraLoop

Copy the files you want into your repository, **after reading the notes below**. They were written by fixed templates from the scan of your project, not by an AI model, and none of them was run against your app. InfraLoop never edits files you already have.

**Your choice:** One Hetzner Cloud server (CPX02: 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM), excl. VAT. The report priced it at about 6.49 EUR/month. Read `SETUP.md` first: it explains in plain words what this choice gives you and what you give up. Then follow `IMPLEMENTATION.md`, which says what to do with these files, step by step.

## `.dockerignore`
.dockerignore for the repository root. Fixes the gap `no_dockerignore`. Confidence: **high**.

Assumed:
- Tests, markdown files and CI config are not needed inside the image.

Check before you use it:
- If your app reads a file that is listed here (for example a README at runtime), remove that line.

## `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
GitHub Actions workflow (build and test). Fixes the gap `no_cicd`. Confidence: **medium**.

Assumed:
- GitHub is the host (the file is a GitHub Actions workflow).
- One job per service folder.

Check before you use it:
- Check the branch name under `on: push` (main is assumed).
- The workflow only builds and tests. It does not deploy anything.
- The last step of each job builds the Docker image from the Dockerfile in that folder.
- Some services have no tests: the workflow only checks that they compile or start installing. Add real tests.

## `.github/dependabot.yml`
Dependabot configuration. Fixes the gap `no_dependency_update_bot`. Confidence: **high**.

Assumed:
- The repository is hosted on GitHub.

Check before you use it:
- The docker entries only matter once a Dockerfile exists in that folder.

## `.env.example`
.env.example (names only). A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **medium**.

Assumed:
- The names come from environment variables the scan found in the code.

Check before you use it:
- Remove names you do not need, and add a short comment for each.
- Make sure .env itself is listed in .gitignore.

## `infra/hetzner/main.tf`
Terraform: server, SSH key and firewall. A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **medium**.

Assumed:
- Ubuntu 24.04 on one server; the firewall opens ports 80 and 443 to everyone and SSH only to `admin_cidrs`.
- The server is created with docker and docker-compose from Ubuntu's own package repository.

Check before you use it:
- Nothing here was run: no `terraform validate`, no server and no container was started. Run `terraform init && terraform validate && terraform plan` before `apply`.
- Hetzner changes server type names and locations over time: check `hcloud server-type list` and edit `server_type` and `location` if needed.
- The Hetzner API token is read from `TF_VAR_hcloud_token`. InfraLoop never asks for it and never stores it.
- Terraform state (`terraform.tfstate`) is created on your machine and can contain sensitive values. It is git-ignored here: keep it that way or move it to a remote backend.

## `infra/hetzner/variables.tf`
Terraform: variables. A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **medium**.

Assumed:
- Server size CPX02 was chosen by the cost estimate in the report; it is not a measured size.

Check before you use it:
- Load-test before you trust the size. The report priced it from the repository's own CPU and memory requests.

## `infra/hetzner/outputs.tf`
Terraform: outputs. A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **high**.

## `infra/hetzner/cloud-init.yaml`
Server start-up script (cloud-init). A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **medium**.

Assumed:
- The repository is public (or readable without a password) and has `docker-compose.prod.yml` on branch `main`.
- The app's environment variables are created as names only, in `/opt/app/.env` on the server.

Check before you use it:
- Fill in the values by logging in: `ssh root@<server_ip>`, edit `/opt/app/.env`, then `cd /opt/app && docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d`.
- The app will not work until you do. This way no secret passes through Terraform state or Hetzner's metadata service.
- Private repository: use a deploy key or build and push an image to a registry instead; this pack does neither.

## `infra/hetzner/terraform.tfvars.example`
Terraform: example values. A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **high**.

## `infra/hetzner/.gitignore`
Keeps Terraform state and your values out of git. A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **high**.

## `docker-compose.prod.yml`
docker-compose file for the server. A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **medium**.

Assumed:
- Each service listens on its template port (app: 8000).
- Only `app` is reachable from outside, through Caddy.

Check before you use it:
- Caddy gets a free HTTPS certificate only when `domain` is set and its DNS record points at the server.
- `caddy:2` follows the latest 2.x release: pin an exact version once it works.
- A database is not part of this file. Add one as another service with a volume, or use a managed database and put its address in `/opt/app/.env`.

## `deploy/Caddyfile`
Reverse proxy configuration. A supporting file for the others (it does not close a gap by itself). Confidence: **medium**.

## Fixes for files you already have

These gaps are about files that exist in your repository. Nothing below was applied: InfraLoop never edits existing files, so make each change by hand.

### Run the container as a non-root user
Gap: `containers_run_as_root`.
Found: all of the 1 analysed Dockerfiles never switch to a non-root USER (e.g. Dockerfile) -- a container escape or app bug then runs with root rights.

1. Add these lines to each Dockerfile listed under Found, after the dependencies are installed and before CMD (Debian or Ubuntu based image):

```dockerfile
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 app
USER app
```

2. On Alpine use `RUN adduser -D -u 10001 app` instead of `useradd`. The official node images already have a user called `node`: use `USER node`.
3. Check that the app can still read its files and only writes where it must (a data or temp folder).

### Create and commit a lock file
Gap: `no_dependency_lockfile`.
Found: Dependency manifests exist but no lock file (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, go.sum...) was found -- installs can resolve to different versions on every build.

1. Run your package manager once and commit the file it creates:
2. Python: `pip-compile` (pip-tools) or `poetry lock`. Node: `npm install` creates package-lock.json. Go: `go mod tidy` creates go.sum.
3. Then switch CI and the Dockerfile to the locked install (`npm ci`, `pip install -r requirements.txt` from the compiled file).

## Not generated

- `no_tests`: Tests need to be written for your code; a generated test would only check that the file exists.
- `no_observability`: Metrics and tracing need a change in your code (a library and an endpoint), not a new file.

files.title: GitHub Actions workflow (build and test)
files.content:
# Generated by InfraLoop from the scan of your repository. Review before use: nothing here was run against your app.
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  app:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      # No tests were found by the scan: add a test step here once you have tests.
      - run: python -m compileall -q .
      - run: docker build -t app:ci .

files.title: Dependabot configuration
files.content:
# Generated by InfraLoop from the scan of your repository. Review before use: nothing here was run against your app.
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "pip"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
  - package-ecosystem: "docker"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"

files.title: Terraform: server, SSH key and firewall
Terraform: variables
Terraform: outputs
Server start-up script (cloud-init)
files.content:
# Generated by InfraLoop from the scan of your repository. Review before use: nothing here was run against your app.
#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages:
  - docker.io
  - docker-compose-v2
  - git
write_files:
  - path: /root/app.env
    permissions: "0600"
    content: |
      ELASTICSEARCH_URL=
      LOG_TO_STDOUT=
      MAIL_PASSWORD=
      MAIL_PORT=
      MAIL_SERVER=
      MAIL_USERNAME=
      MAIL_USE_TLS=
      MS_TRANSLATOR_KEY=
      REDIS_URL=
      SECRET_KEY=
      SERVER_NAME=
      SITE_ADDRESS=${site_address}
runcmd:
  - systemctl enable --now docker
  - git clone --branch ${branch} ${repo_url} /opt/app
  - sh -c 'cd /opt/app && { [ -f .env ] || cp /root/app.env .env; }'
  - sh -c 'cd /opt/app && docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d --build'

files.title: Terraform: example values
files.content:
# Copy to terraform.tfvars and fill in. terraform.tfvars is git-ignored: keep it that way.
# The API token does NOT go here. Export it instead:  export TF_VAR_hcloud_token=...
ssh_public_key = "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@example.com"
admin_cidrs    = ["203.0.113.4/32"]   # your own public address
repo_url       = "https://github.com/YOU/YOUR-REPO.git"
# branch      = "main"
# domain      = "app.example.com"
# backups     = true

files.title: Keeps Terraform state and your values out of git
docker-compose file for the server
files.content:
# Generated by InfraLoop from the scan of your repository. Review before use: nothing here was run against your app.
services:
  app:
    build: .
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file: .env
    expose: ["8000"]
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports: ["80:80", "443:443"]
    environment:
      SITE_ADDRESS: ${SITE_ADDRESS:-:80}
    volumes:
      - ./deploy/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config
    depends_on: [app]
volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:
